Electrical discharge machining studies that focus on graphite electrodes report consistent relationships between electrode microstructure, process parameters, and machining outcomes for Hastelloy. Nowicki et al. (2022) found that graphite with larger grains increased process efficiency (higher MRR) but returned greater relative tool wear, while finer-grained graphite produced the lowest surface roughness; discharge current and pulse duration were the principal drivers of MRR and Ra, and the time interval most influenced relative electrode wear in their experiments on Hastelloy C-22. (Nowicki et al. 2022) The later work by Nowicki et al. (2024) reinforces these conclusions and extends them for negative polarity EDM: fine-grained POCO AF-5 ($1\ \mu$m$)$ improves efficiency and reduces tool wear compared with coarser POCO EDM-180 ($10\ \mu$m$)$, and detached graphite grains alter discharge stability and thus process effectiveness. (Nowicki et al. 2024)

Across studies of nickel-based and corrosion-resistant superalloys, peak current and pulse-on time repeatedly emerge as dominant electrical factors controlling both MRR and surface quality. Nas & Kara (2022) reported peak current as the most influential parameter on MRR and Ra, accounting for the largest share of variance in their Taguchi–ANOVA analysis, and identified cryogenic treatment, pulse-on time and peak current as the triad most affecting machinability in their factorial tests. (Nas & Kara 2022) Complementary experimental work on other nickel alloys shows current and pulse duration strongly affect electrode geometry and wear patterns: Ramabalan et al. (2024) observed that those two factors largely determine electrode taper, edge rounding and wear length when producing square holes in Hastelloy B2. (Ramabalan et al. 2024)

Broader reviews of EDM performance and enhancement techniques place these parameter effects in context and point to multiple routes for reducing TWR and improving MRR. Shastri et al. (2022) summarize that EDM’s main limitations (high TWR, low MRR and elevated roughness) have been addressed experimentally by combinations such as cryogenic treatment, powder-mixed dielectrics and ultrasonic assistance, each altering the measured MRR, TWR and surface integrity in different ways. (Shastri et al. 2022) Work on dielectric modifications and electrode treatments likewise shows practical gains: Sana et al. (2024) report that nanopowder in the dielectric and cryogenic treatment of electrodes produced large reductions in electrode wear and dimensional overcut for brass electrodes in their experiments. (Sana et al. 2024) General method surveys highlight the potential to tailor coatings or EDC-like approaches to influence surface layers formed during EDM, which may be relevant when selecting electrode materials. (Liew et al. 2020)

Despite this body of evidence, direct comparative data that evaluate copper versus graphite versus composite electrodes specifically on Hastelloy (MRR, TWR, and parameter sensitivities) are not present in the cited sources.
rows.b:
Graphite with a larger grain size produced higher material removal rates but also greater relative tool wear when machining Hastelloy C-22, while finer-grained graphite yielded lower surface roughness; these outcomes derive from experiments comparing POCO AF-5 (1 µm) and S-180 (10 µm) electrodes. (Nowicki et al. 2022) The same contrast is reported in a later evaluation using the same POCO materials under negative polarity, which attributes improved process efficiency and reduced tool wear to fine-grained graphite and notes that detached graphite grains disturb discharge stability and machining efficiency. (Nowicki et al. 2024) Both studies modelled the relationships between machining parameters and outcomes, indicating that discharge current and pulse duration principally govern MRR and Ra for the graphite electrodes tested. (Nowicki et al. 2022)(Nowicki et al. 2024)

Peak current dominated effects on MRR and average surface roughness in a Taguchi-designed factorial study of a corrosion-resistant superalloy subjected to different cryogenic treatments, accounting for 86.43% of MRR variance and 74.79% of Ra variance in ANOVA results. (Nas & Kara 2022) Experimental investigations of Hastelloy B2 report that current and pulse duration substantially affect electrode wear, with unstable sparks causing electrode ends to transform from sharp to hemispherical shapes as heat diffuses and edges erode. (Ramabalan et al. 2024)(Nas & Kara 2022) Regression and ANOVA analyses from titanium EDM work likewise identify amperage (current) as the single most influential factor for MRR and TWR, with percentages near 99% for several response variables. (Akıncıoğlu 2022)

Methods intended to reduce tool wear or alter surface integrity during EDM include cryogenic treatment, powder-mixed dielectrics, ultrasonic assistance, and electrical discharge coating; reviews synthesize evidence that these associations change MRR, TWR, surface roughness and recast layer characteristics. (Shastri et al. 2022)(Liew et al. 2020) For example, adding nanopowder to the dielectric and applying cryogenic treatment to electrodes produced substantial reductions in electrode wear and overcut for brass electrodes in experimental studies, with reported improvements up to around 78% for EWR and 81% for dimensional accuracy depending on conditions. (Sana et al. 2024) These interventions show that electrode material condition and dielectric composition interact with peak current, pulse-on time and spark voltage to modify wear and removal outcomes. (Sana et al. 2024)(Shastri et al. 2022)

Taken together, the cited literature establishes that electrode material microstructure (graphite grain size), electrical parameters (particularly current and pulse duration), and auxiliary treatments (cryogenic processing, powder-mixed dielectric, coatings) each alter MRR, TWR and surface quality in EDM of nickel-based alloys, while direct experimental comparisons involving composite electrodes on Hastelloy are not provided in the assembled sources. (Nowicki et al. 2022)(Nowicki et al. 2024)(Nas & Kara 2022)(Shastri et al. 2022)

The additive manufacturing route imposed by selective laser melting (SLM) produces a characteristic fine martensitic microstructure and very small grain/subgrain dimensions in 18Ni-300 maraging steel, reflecting the extremely high cooling rates during layer-wise melting and solidification. Tan et al. observed an average submicron grain size of $0.31\ \mu$m in SLM-fabricated grade 300 maraging steel and reported a martensitic matrix containing dense, needle-like Ni$_3$X precipitates (X = Ti, Al, Mo) that develop during the process and subsequent thermal treatments; these features were linked to age hardening and to residual-stress states generated by rapid solidification. (Tan et al. 2018) Ahmadkhaniha et al. likewise found a fine-grained martensitic structure in the as-printed condition and reported similar microstructural appearance across different section planes (xy, xz, yz), with no pronounced crystallographic texture or anisotropy in the as-built material. (Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021) The SLM process can therefore be regarded as producing near-full-density components with an intrinsically refined martensitic microstructure. (Yap et al. 2015)

Thermal post-processing substantially modifies these as-built states. Systematic heat treatments relieve residual stress, promote precipitation, and change mechanical anisotropy, while specific intercritical treatments can induce phase reversion. Tan et al. showed that designed heat treatments both increase strengthening by precipitate evolution and reduce residual stress and mechanical anisotropy compared with as-fabricated specimens. (Tan et al. 2018) Godec et al. examined the interaction of solution treatment, aging and subsequent plasma nitriding, finding that prior heat treatments alter the morphology and chemistry of surface compound layers and affect properties after thermo-chemical treatments. (Godec et al. 2021)

Austenite reversion in maraging steels processed by SLM is reported to occur when specimens are tempered near the austenite formation range, producing reversed austenite that nucleates preferentially at martensite lath boundaries where Ni enrichment occurs. (Khan et al. 2022) Khan et al. tempered selective-laser-melted maraging steel in the intercritical $\alpha' + \gamma$ range (about $720\ ^\circ$C in their study) and observed reversed austenite along lath boundaries; they attributed its nucleation to local Ni enrichment following dissolution of intermetallic particles. (Khan et al. 2022) That study further links the presence of reversed austenite to improved pitting resistance in chloride solution, reporting higher pitting potentials and lower corrosion current densities for the 720°C-tempered specimens compared with as-printed, aged, and homogenized counterparts. (Khan et al. 2022)

Corrosion behaviour in chloride environments has been assessed in several works, with corrosion performance influenced by microstructure, precipitates, surface condition and post-treatments. Khan et al. evaluated pitting in 3.5 wt% NaCl and found that reversed austenite raised the pitting potential and reduced corrosion rate compared with other heat-treatment states. (Khan et al. 2022) Ahmadkhaniha et al. compared corrosion of SLM and wrought maraging steels and reported that, despite finer as-printed microstructure, corrosion behaviour after heat treatment and aging was similar between SLM and conventional wrought material; they also identified precipitation as a primary factor controlling both hardness and corrosion response, and showed that electropolishing markedly reduces surface roughness. (Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021) Godec et al. linked prior heat treatments to improved corrosion resistance after plasma nitriding and noted that omitting appropriate prior aging can lead to defects (cracks, pores) in compound nitride layers that compromise performance. (Godec et al. 2021)
rows.b:
(Tan et al. 2018)reports a submicron grain size of $0.31\ \mu\text{m}$ in SLM-produced grade 300 maraging steel, which the authors attribute to cooling rates on the order of $10^{7}\ \text{K/s}$ during processing. (Tan et al. 2018) This extreme refinement coincides with a martensitic matrix containing dense, needle-shaped Ni3X precipitates that develop in the as-fabricated state and that contribute to age hardening; electron microscopy in that study resolves the precipitate–matrix interfaces and supports an Orowan/coherency strain interpretation of strengthening. (Tan et al. 2018) Haghdadi et al. 2020 summarise that such unique hierarchical (sub)grains and fine precipitates are characteristic of AM steels and that these features can increase strength, wear resistance and corrosion resistance relative to conventional counterparts. (Haghdadi et al. 2020)

(Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021)finds that the as-printed SLM maraging steel exhibits a fine-grained martensitic structure with a surface roughness $R_a\approx 10\ \mu\text{m}$ and no marked texture or anisotropy across the XY, XZ and YZ sections. (Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021) In that work, aging produces the highest nano-hardness and shifts the corrosion potential to lower values, and the authors conclude that precipitation governs both hardness and corrosion behaviour; electropolishing reduced $R_a$ by about 65%. (Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021) Afkhami et al. note that processing parameters including build orientation and heat treatment affect mechanical performance, implying similar process sensitivity for microstructure and derived properties in SLM steels. (Afkhami et al. 2019)

(Khan et al. 2022)reports that tempering within the intercritical $\alpha'+\gamma$ range at $720\ ^\circ\text{C}$ produces reversed austenite that nucleates mainly along martensite lath boundaries; local Ni enrichment from dissolved intermetallics promotes this reversion. (Khan et al. 2022) The same study directly links the presence of this reversed austenite to improved pitting resistance in 3.5 wt% NaCl: the $720\ ^\circ\text{C}$-tempered specimen exhibits a higher pitting potential, a lower corrosion current density, and a lower corrosion rate than as-printed, aged, or homogenized specimens lacking reversed austenite. (Khan et al. 2022) Khan et al. therefore conclude that austenite reversion can enhance pitting resistance in SLM maraging steel under chloride exposure. (Khan et al. 2022)

(Godec et al. 2021)shows that when SLM 18Ni-300 is plasma nitrided without prior aging, cracks form in the compound nitride layer, whereas specimens given prior heat treatment before nitriding show improved wear and corrosion resistance and fewer defects in the nitrided layer. (Godec et al. 2021) Yan et al. compare SLM and cold-spray composites and report that SLM produces higher densification and lower porosity, which in the SLM case correlates with a lower wear rate and more stable friction behaviour; microstructural evolution of reinforcements is cited as the cause of these property differences. (Yan et al. 2018) Collectively, these studies indicate that SLM’s intrinsic microstructural state and subsequent heat or thermo-chemical treatments strongly control surface layer quality and chloride-environment corrosion performance. (Godec et al. 2021)(Yan et al. 2018)

Household decisions about rooftop photovoltaic (PV) systems are shaped by interlinked financial, informational and institutional barriers that studies identify as central impediments to adoption. Multiple empirical analyses highlight that the upfront cost and concerns about returns form a primary inhibitor: Parsad et al. found that government subsidies reduce the perceived initial risk of investment and that low prices and maintenance costs function as financial motivators by easing long‑term return anxieties. (Parsad et al. 2020) Tanveer et al. report that perceived cost has a negative effect on consumers' willingness to adopt solar PV, reinforcing the centrality of price as a barrier in household choices. (Tanveer et al. 2021) Aarakit et al. also conclude that affordability determines the type of solar product households choose, and they recommend flexible payment mechanisms to enable income‑constrained households to acquire more expensive systems. (Aarakit et al. 2021)

Parsad et al. emphasise the role of PV subsidies as the primary motivator for household investment, placing policy interventions at the core of uptake strategies. (Parsad et al. 2020) Goel situates rooftop PV targets within national ambitions (India’s solar goals and rooftop share are a policy driver for deployment), while also documenting the challenges in translating national targets into local installations. (Goel 2016) Kappagantu et al. examined a pilot smart‑grid project and reported implementation barriers encountered by consumers in that local programme context, indicating that project‑level design affects how households experience policy measures. (Kappagantu et al. 2015)

Beyond finance and formal incentives, lack of knowledge and technical concerns reduce adoption likelihood. Parsad et al. identify technical barriers and deficits in knowledge and awareness as significant predictors of investment decisions, with these non‑financial factors carrying weight alongside economic evaluations. (Parsad et al. 2020) Tanveer et al. similarly find that perceptions of self‑efficacy and beliefs about PV benefits increase willingness to adopt, whereas perceived risk decreases it, indicating that households’ subjective assessments of technology risks and capabilities influence uptake. (Tanveer et al. 2021) Sovacool et al. broaden this view by showing that equity and justice dimensions (demographic and spatial disparities among others) shape who can access household solar and under what conditions, implying that informational and social barriers intersect with broader distributional concerns. (Sovacool et al. 2022)

Country‑ and context‑specific constraints further mediate barriers to adoption. Reviews of renewable energy in India highlight structural constraints that must be resolved to exploit the country's solar potential, suggesting that favourable resource endowments alone do not remove impediments to deployment. (Khare et al. 2013) Likewise, sectoral reviews point to institutional, market and investment challenges that policymakers and stakeholders must address to scale rooftop PV. (J & Majid 2020) These findings collectively indicate that overcoming household hesitation requires a combination of price‑reducing finance, targeted subsidies, flexible payment options, improved technical information and attention to equity and local implementation dynamics. (Parsad et al. 2020)(Aarakit et al. 2021)(Sovacool et al. 2022)
rows.b:
India's policy target allocates 40 GW of the planned 100 GW solar capacity to grid-connected rooftop PV, framing rooftop deployment as a central element of national renewable goals. (Goel 2016) This national commitment shapes the policy instruments and incentives studied in the literature and provides the policy context within which household barriers are assessed. (Goel 2016)

In survey data from Kerala, government subsidies emerge as the primary financial motivator that reduces the initial investment risk for households considering PV adoption. (Parsad et al. 2020) The same Kerala study finds that lower purchase prices and reduced maintenance costs act as additional financial motivators by alleviating long-run return concerns. (Parsad et al. 2020) Using SEM followed by an ANN ranking, the authors also identify technical barriers and gaps in knowledge and awareness as significant predictors of household investment decisions. (Parsad et al. 2020)

A multi-city household questionnaire in Pakistan reports that higher perceived cost and greater perceived risk both reduce willingness to adopt rooftop PV. (Tanveer et al. 2021) That study also shows that social norms and perceived self-efficacy increase willingness to adopt, while openness to technology did not exert a measurable effect in their sample. (Tanveer et al. 2021) Together these findings indicate that both economic assessments and psychosocial perceptions influence household choices in ways that complement the Kerala results. (Parsad et al. 2020)(Tanveer et al. 2021)

Evidence from Uganda indicates affordability and payment flexibility shape not only whether households adopt solar but also which product types they choose. (Aarakit et al. 2021) In that nationally representative analysis, flexible payment mechanisms increase uptake of solar home systems and kits, while access to grid electricity is negatively associated with adoption of those off-grid products. (Aarakit et al. 2021) The Uganda results therefore link financing modalities and existing service availability to heterogeneous adoption outcomes across rural and urban households. (Aarakit et al. 2021)

A pilot smart-grid project survey in Puducherry identifies concrete implementation issues at the consumer level, including available roof space and users’ practical experiences with rooftop systems, as constraints discussed alongside government initiatives. (Kappagantu et al. 2015) Reviews of India-wide renewable deployment underline a broader set of obstacles to scaling renewables that policy and industry must address. (J & Majid 2020) Complementing these India-focused studies, a mixed-methods review of household solar highlights multiple inequities (demographic, spatial, interspecies and temporal) that can be associated with rapid solar expansion and that interact with the barriers above. (Sovacool et al. 2022)

Several studies therefore converge on a core pattern: upfront cost, inadequate financing options, and subsidy design materially affect adoption, while technical, informational, and equity-related barriers modulate uptake across places and populations. (Parsad et al. 2020)(Aarakit et al. 2021)

Evidence on the clinical impact of diabetes self-management apps is mixed and context-dependent. A pragmatic multicentre randomized trial of the BlueStar app found no difference in HbA1c between intervention and control arms at three months when analysed by allocation, though an exploratory within-user analysis indicated that each additional day of app use was associated with a small reduction in 3‑month HbA1c ($0.016$ points per day of use, 95% CI $-0.03$ to $-0.003$). (Agarwal et al. 2018) The same trial reported substantial variation in engagement between sites, with median days of login ranging from 9 to 36 over 14 weeks, suggesting that setting and implementation factors strongly influence both use and any downstream clinical effects. (Agarwal et al. 2018)

Shorter, user-centred pilots provide complementary evidence on mechanisms linking app features to self-management behaviours. In a 12‑week pilot of a gamified app for adolescents with type 1 diabetes, automated transfer of glucometer readings, immediate trend analysis with suggested causes and remedies, and rewards increased average daily blood glucose checks by 50% (from 2.4 to 3.6 per day, $P=.006$). (Cafazzo et al. 2012) The authors caution, however, that improved monitoring frequency does not automatically translate into HbA1c improvement unless incentives are connected to decision-making and corrective actions triggered by the data. (Cafazzo et al. 2012)

Systematic and qualitative syntheses identify recurring design and contextual determinants of effectiveness and sustained use. A review of health‑behavior app trials reported that most included studies showed behavior change in the intended direction and that retention in intervention groups was frequently 60%–100%; the review highlights common features associated with better outcomes: reduced time burden, intuitive design, real‑time feedback, personalization, detailed information and involvement of health professionals. (Zhao et al. 2016) Qualitative work mapping users’ perceptions distilled nine themes affecting adoption and continued use, including barriers, motivators, credibility, personalization, reminders and sharing preferences. (Peng et al. 2016) Interviews with adults with type 2 diabetes reinforced these points: users value visual trend displays, easy navigation and convenience, while non‑users often lack awareness or professional recommendation; participants recommended stronger educational content, dynamic monitoring with tips, and nutrition support. (Jeffrey et al. 2019)

App inventories and quality appraisals show gaps between typical commercial offerings and the features users and trials associate with sustained benefit. A content comparison of store apps found most prioritized reporting and reminders over personalised education or therapeutic support, with only a minority scoring highly across core self‑management features. (Izahar et al. 2017) Broader reviews of the app ecosystem warn about variable quality and call for consumer education, connectivity standards, and mechanisms for certification or vetting to protect users and guide selection. (Boulos et al. 2014)

Together, the evidence indicates that app‑driven improvements in self‑management behaviours are feasible, but translation into consistent HbA1c gains depends on real‑world engagement, app design that links data to actionable decisions, and supportive implementation contexts such as clinician endorsement and site‑level facilitation. (Cafazzo et al. 2012)(Agarwal et al. 2018)(Zhao et al. 2016)
rows.b:
In a pragmatic randomized trial, there was no difference between intervention and control arms in HbA1c at 3 months, with an adjusted mean difference of −0.42 (95% CI −1.05 to 0.21; P =.19). (Agarwal et al. 2018) Each additional day of app use in an exploratory analysis was associated with a small reduction in 3‑month HbA1c of 0.016 percentage points (95% CI −0.03 to −0.003), indicating a dose–response association between app engagement and short‑term glycaemic change within users. (Agarwal et al. 2018) The trial also shows that app usage varied markedly between clinical sites, with median days used ranging from 9 to 36 over 14 weeks, suggesting contextual influences on engagement. (Agarwal et al. 2018)

A synthesis of app-based behaviour‑change trials found that 17 of 23 included studies reported statistically significant changes in targeted health behaviours, and that 19 studies had retention in the intervention group of at least 60%, with the range of retention reported as 60%–100%. (Zhao et al. 2016)

In qualitative work, participants identified nine thematic determinants of adoption and continued use, including barriers, motivators, credibility, personalised guidance, tracking, reminders and sharing features. (Peng et al. 2016) Complementary interviews with people living with type 2 diabetes found that visual trend displays, intuitive navigation and convenience facilitate use, while lack of awareness, limited clinician endorsement, low technological or health literacy, and practical issues such as poor rural connectivity hinder uptake. (Jeffrey et al. 2019) Participants recommended stronger educational content, dynamic monitoring with tips, nutritional support and clinician involvement as design priorities to improve engagement. (Jeffrey et al. 2019)

A content survey of commercial diabetes apps showed that most offerings emphasised reporting and reminders rather than personalised education or therapeutic support, with only a minority of apps scoring highly across eight evaluated self‑management features. (Izahar et al. 2017) The same assessment observed that many apps were free, small in size, and usable offline, but that functional design often neglects integrated, tailored disease management features. (Izahar et al. 2017)

A review of the app ecosystem highlighted the large and rapidly growing number of health apps and persistent concerns about quality, safety, interoperability and the need for consumer education and regulatory oversight. (Boulos et al. 2014) Prior pilots in younger populations showed that gamified reward mechanisms can increase monitoring frequency (an increase from 2.4 to 3.6 measurements per day in one pilot), but authors cautioned that improved monitoring alone may not translate to HbA1c reductions without incentives that link monitoring to decision‑making. (Cafazzo et al. 2012)

Research that evaluates microfinance-supported entrepreneurship finds mixed but informative patterns regarding business outcomes and broader empowerment. Quantitative comparisons in a quasi-experimental design show that women running microfinance-backed businesses display stronger economic and psychological indicators than comparable non-entrepreneur women, though gains on political and social indicators are smaller or absent; qualitative interviews in the same study reinforced the conclusion that entrepreneurship contributes to holistic empowerment while also revealing social empowerment among some non-entrepreneurs. (Khan et al. 2022) Studies that synthesize the broader microfinance literature likewise stress heterogeneity in objectives and outcomes across institutions and programs, noting that sustainability, products, management and targeting shape who benefits and how. (Brau & Woller 2004)

A long-term quasi-experiment in rural India finds that access to ICT and the structure of women's social networks substantially affect entry into entrepreneurship and firm performance: family and community ties amplify the benefits of ICT for establishing and profiting from new businesses, while ties to local male powerholders can constrain ICT’s positive effects unless those ties are weak. (Venkatesh et al. 2017) Complementary evidence from work on social entrepreneurship shows that business processes designed to align with prevailing cultural norms can enable women’s economic participation while also shifting social relations, indicating that organizational design and norm-sensitive practices matter alongside finance. (Haugh & Talwar 2014) Case studies of women owner-managers in tourism likewise document how combining community-serving social objectives with commercial strategies shapes developmental impacts beyond mere access to funds. (Kimbu & Ngoasong 2016)

Critical analyses question whether credit alone achieves intended poverty-alleviation or empowerment goals. Ethnographic research in Bangladeshi villages reports that microfinance can increase indebtedness and exacerbate vulnerabilities, and that market-based interventions may undermine the social capital needed for durable entrepreneurial capability. (Banerjee & Jackson 2016) At the industry level, observers argue that commercialisation and profit-seeking change which customers can be reached: institutions with explicit social missions, often supported by subsidies, appear better placed to serve the poorest clients than purely profit-driven lenders. (Cull et al. 2009)

Conceptual work clarifies why outcomes vary over time and context by proposing a three-dimensional framing of empowerment (personal, relational and societal) and by emphasizing that cultural setting and timing of evaluation affect which dimensions show change. (Huis et al. 2017) Taken together, the evidence indicates that microcredit can facilitate business creation and some dimensions of empowerment, but that firm-level supports, information and communication technologies, social-network context, culturally attuned business models, and institutional design markedly influence whether credit translates into sustained enterprise growth and deeper social or political empowerment. (Khan et al. 2022)(Venkatesh et al. 2017)(Haugh & Talwar 2014)
rows.b:
Venkatesh et al. report that 160 new businesses opened in intervention villages versus 40 in controls over seven years, showing large increases in entrepreneurial activity associated with an ICT intervention. (Venkatesh et al. 2017) These gains are concentrated among women with strong ties to family and community and high ICT use, indicating that business formation and persistence depend on social-network context as well as access to tools. (Venkatesh et al. 2017) Khan et al. find that women who are entrepreneurs score higher on economic, psychological and some relational indicators than non-entrepreneurs in their sample, supporting the association between entrepreneurship and improved household economic position. (Khan et al. 2022) Haugh and Talwar find that business processes shaped to fit local norms can expand women’s economic activity while also interacting with social structures, suggesting that culturally attuned business models affect who can translate finance into viable enterprises. (Haugh & Talwar 2014)

Khan et al. observe that the measurable gains for entrepreneurs are smaller or absent for political and social empowerment in their study area, indicating uneven effects across domains of empowerment. (Khan et al. 2022) Huis et al. synthesize evidence into a Three-Dimensional Model that distinguishes personal, relational, and societal empowerment and argues that time and culture alter when and which dimensions respond to interventions. (Huis et al. 2017) Taken together, these findings imply that microfinance- enabled entrepreneurship tends to change individual-level beliefs and some household interactions before broader social or political outcomes appear. (Khan et al. 2022)(Huis et al. 2017)

Banerjee and Jackson document that introducing microfinance to poor communities can increase indebtedness and weaken social capital, highlighting pathways by which credit alone can harm rather than help livelihoods. (Banerjee & Jackson 2016) Cull et al. argue from industry-wide data that commercialization and market forces alter which clients are served and that subsidies and mission-driven institutions remain crucial to reach the poorest; this points to institutional limits of relying solely on credit markets to deliver broad development impacts. (Cull et al. 2009) Brau and Woller note that microfinance research has not yet fully entered mainstream entrepreneurial finance debates, implying gaps in understanding how financial products translate into sustainable business growth. (Brau & Woller 2004)

Venkatesh et al. additionally show that ICT amplified the positive effects of social ties on entrepreneurship, with interaction effects that evolve over time. (Venkatesh et al. 2017) Qualitative studies of social and tourism sector enterprises indicate that women combine social objectives and commercial strategies to serve community needs, suggesting that complementary interventions (network strengthening, culturally aligned business models, and ICT) modify whether and how credit becomes productive. (Haugh & Talwar 2014)(Kimbu & Ngoasong 2016)
